## 1. The question, frozen
The paper answers many things (the orbital fit, the number density, the spin state). The title and first sentence make one central: *Is 'Oumuamua a natural object — a planetesimal or its fragment, explained by known minor bodies and planet-formation theory — rather than an artificial one?* Range: the object's observed properties and the population it belongs to. What is asked: mostly backward ("what can we tell from what we see?"), with a comparative edge against a rival. Held fixed for the run.

## 2. The explanation in parts (owner's words)
P1 It originated as a planetesimal (or fragment) ejected from a planetary system. P2 Its non-gravitational acceleration (radial, 1/r²) is outgassing (H₂O plus another volatile). P3 Its shape is an elongated ellipsoid (≥6:1). P4 Its light curve is shape-dominated, not albedo. P5 Its number density ≈0.1 au⁻³ follows from a mass density times a size-frequency distribution (SFD). P6 Its trajectory is what is expected of detectable *inactive* interstellar objects. P7 Its red colour is a normal minor-body surface. P8 The missing dust and gas mean an extinct, devolatilised body, or large grains, or a thermal lag. P9 The comparison set (67P, 2P/Encke, 96P, C/2016 R2, Manx objects).

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Because |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Held if | Removing it breaks "where did it come from." But that job leans on the mass-budget assumptions, themselves fitted. The *route* is loose: six mechanisms (Fig. 2) each produce an ejected planetesimal. |
| P2 | Held | By the 1/r² radial fit with A₁=(4.92±0.16)×10⁻⁶ m/s², and because the nearest swap (solar radiation pressure) needs a density 3–4 orders too low. That swap stays alive only through the fractal-aggregate patch. |
| P3 | Loose | Six routes give elongation; none matches 6:1 self-consistently (the paper's own open question). Any would do. |
| P4 | Held | By the V-shaped minima and broad maxima; a swap to patchy albedo does not yield that light-curve shape. |
| P5 | Two routes / held if | Several SFDs (e.g. b2, or a high mass density) reach the measured density — either route does the job. It is *held if* the "SFD is known" job holds, and the paper itself says it isn't, from one detection. |
| P6 | Held | The strongest part. Built and published as a prediction (Engelhardt 2017) eight months *before* discovery; the observed elements sit at the predicted peak for inactive objects (Fig. 4). |
| P7 | Loose | Colour is "not diagnostic": organics, iron-rich minerals, space weathering all give it. |
| P8 | Held if / borrowed | Held only by the doubtful job "outgassing happens but leaves no trace," patched by large grains, thermal lag, prior devolatilisation. Those patches are borrowed from comet behaviour not tested here, and the large-grain patch has no gauge. |
| P9 | Borrowed | The whole comparison set rests on Solar System comet behaviour this paper cites but does not test. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks
**Flip.** Had 'Oumuamua shown a dust tail or detected gas, the same natural story would have covered it — natural comets do exactly that. So the dust/gas job explains both outcomes and holds nothing. The trajectory and density jobs *do* bite: an inactive object at these elements was predicted.
**Direction.** Almost all backward. The Fig. 4 prediction is the one forward step.
**Answer in the starting points.** The mass budget *assumes* each gas-giant system ejects 1–100 M⊕ and each ice-giant system 0.1–10 M⊕; the conclusion ("enough ejecta exist") sits close to that assumption. It is honestly given a wide range, but part of the answer is carried in the start.
**Jobs from.** Nearly all jobs are the owner's (given). The ones I added: why *large* dust, why no home system, why not detected earlier.
**Pairs that pull.** (a) "extinct/devolatilised" versus "still outgassing enough to accelerate" — the paper gives way on the first. (b) "no dust" versus "outgassing makes dust." (c) "unusually elongated and rare" versus "common enough to be detected." Each passes alone; together they strain.
**Catch-alls.** "Another volatile species," "some comets are depleted," "large grains" can absorb a failed detection. Only the dust limit (<1.7×10⁻³ kg/s) comes with a gauge, and it does not reach large grains — so that catch-all has no gauge.
**Change list leaves out,** openly: pre-perihelion data (so outgassing symmetry is assumed), large-grain sensitivity, the pole orientation, the SFD, the home system.
**Rivals.** The alien solar sail passes the shape job but fails one the natural story does cheaply: the light curve needs a changing orientation while the sail needs a fixed one. The fractal aggregate survives on paper but "has never been detected." No change on the list separates the six natural routes — at this level they are one explanation.
**Where parts came from.** Fig. 4: built, and tested before the fact. The outgassing scaling from 67P: fitted. "Natural" itself: asserted until a rival is compared.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary
(1) A radio/large-grain search — it would give the "large grains" catch-all the gauge it lacks. (2) More interstellar objects to fix the SFD — this turns P5 from *held if* to *held*. (3) A measured pole orientation — this turns "cigar or oblate" from *loose* to *held*.

## 6. What this does not show
Hard to vary is not the same as true. The natural origin could still be wrong. Passing means only that some parts (elements, density, light-curve shape) are held by checkable jobs, not that 'Oumuamua is a planetesimal.

## 7. One next step
Run the missing-gauge poke: a large-grain (radio) search. The claim already predicts "outgassing with only large grains," so the prediction is written down in advance and the search can catch it out.
